_about: The /pathway page: three routes into cancer care, the gap at each step, its evidence and the Silta bands. Read by app/templates/_pathway.html and app/static/pathway.js. Numbers from brain sources/2026-11-14-cancerregistry-screening-by-language.md, sources/2026-11-14-europepmc-unmet-need-and-access-by-origin.md, sources/2026-11-14-espoo-equity-talk-kuitunen.md, sources/2026-11-13-web-research-minorities-screening.md and notes/2026-11-14-0145-silta-deep-data-analysis.md. Each step's `silta` text is kept for a later Silta section and is not shown in the top panel.

page.title: Where people fall out of cancer care
page.lede: People reach cancer care through a screening letter, a symptom they notice, or a test a doctor orders. On each route, people whose native language is not Finnish, Swedish or Sámi meet gaps that Silta is built for. Only the screening route is measured by language, and there the gap is large.
page.prompt: Select a step on the map to see the gap and its evidence.
limitations: Only 3 of the 11 steps are recorded by native language, all of them in screening. Beyond screening we rely on studies grouped by origin or care sector, and some steps have no data at all.
“Other native language” pools many languages and includes people whose language is unknown. We use native language as a proxy for needing language support, which it only approximates.

Language, education and region of birth overlap. Across about 290 municipalities, language still predicts lower breast and colorectal attendance after controlling for education, age, urbanisation and unemployment. This is an area-level model and does not prove cause.

The symptom-route figures come from one lymphoma study (160 patients) and two surveys grouped by origin (2010–12 and 2018–19). They show which way the gap runs, not how large it is for the people Silta serves.

We show a difference only when its 95% confidence interval excludes zero. This left out colposcopy after an abnormal cervical result (+2.3 percentage points, not significant), waiting times (county medians, not tested by language) and digital-clinic contact rates (descriptive only). Attendance by region of birth is shown as published, without a test.
sources: Finnish Cancer Registry, mass-screening statistics by native language, region of birth and previous result, 2020–2024 (published 20 May 2026).
Kuusio et al., BMC Health Services Research 2022 (FinMonik 2018–19), doi:10.1186/s12913-022-08155-3.
Norwegian randomised trial of invitations in the language of origin.
National Cancer Strategy 2026–2035, Goal 3 and sub-goals 1.3 and 2.5.
All captured in the team knowledge base (madviking/junction2026, sources/ and notes/).

Doctor visit and referral, private or occupational care

bands.name: Find
bands.text: Official Finnish health information in the person's own language, such as what a screening letter means or what a symptom may need.

bands.name: Prepare
bands.text: Describe what you noticed by voice, tapping or writing. It is a checklist, not a diagnosis.

bands.name: Navigate
bands.text: Who to call in the person's county and what to expect. It adds a Finnish call script to read aloud and a reminder of the right to a free professional interpreter.

bands.name: At the visit
bands.text: A visit card and flash cards show symptoms and questions with very little Finnish.

bands.name: For the clinician
bands.text: A one-screen Finnish summary, preferences known in advance, and a prompt to offer a home self-sampling kit when cervical screening is overdue.

bands.name: After the visit
bands.text: Tells people what happens next, how long it usually takes, and when to call if nothing arrives.

letter.title: Everything starts with a letter
letter.text: In 2024 the three programmes invited 78,914 people whose native language is not Finnish, Swedish or Sámi. Translation alone does not help. In a Norwegian randomised trial, letters in the person's own language gave 46.5% attendance, against 47.4% for standard letters.
letter.silta: Scanning the QR code on the letter opens Silta. It explains the letter in the person's language and says what to do next.
letter.src: Finnish Cancer Registry, native-language tables 2024; Norwegian randomised trial of language-of-origin invitations.

attend.title: Attendance is 21 points lower
attend.text: 57% of other-language invitees attended screening in 2024, against 78% of Finnish, Swedish and Sámi speakers. The gap is about the same in all three programmes. Few people who miss a round come back.
notes: All gaps are significant. “All three” is pooled from invitee counts. The national target is 80% attendance in every programme, with no difference by native language.
The breast and cervical gaps widened from 2020 to 2024 (breast +2.5 percentage points, 95% CI 1.6–3.4; cervical +4.2, 3.4–5.0).
Of people who missed a colorectal round, about 18% attend the next one; of previous attenders, 91–93% do.
Attendance by region of birth is shown as the registry publishes it, without a significance test.
attend.silta: It explains the test and how to book or rebook, with flash cards to show at the appointment.
attend.src: Finnish Cancer Registry, native language, region of birth and previous-result tables 2020–2024; two-proportion tests; National Cancer Strategy 2026–2035.

follow.title: Fewer complete follow-up after a positive test
follow.text: 68% of other-language invitees had a colonoscopy after a positive stool test, against 77% (2022–24). After an abnormal cervical result, the difference is not significant.
notes: Pooled over 2022–24 because yearly groups are small (about 370–500 positive tests a year). The 95% CI of the gap is 6.3–11.3 points.
In the 2022 round, 87 colorectal cancers were found in people who tested positive but never had the colonoscopy.
Breast follow-up is reported only as a referral rate.
follow.silta: What a colonoscopy is, how to prepare for it, and when to call if no appointment has arrived.
follow.src: Finnish Cancer Registry, native-language tables 2022–2024; colorectal interval cancers, 2022 round.

notice.title: Recognising that a symptom matters
notice.text: No register records when a symptom starts, so this step cannot be measured for anyone. For cancers without screening, such as lung cancer, it is the only way in.
notice.silta: “I noticed something” gives official guidance in the person's language. It does not diagnose.

contact.title: Knowing where to go
contact.text: People of foreign origin depend far more on municipal health centres, report more unmet need for a doctor's care and are less satisfied with access. The surveys grouped people by origin, not language, and did not look at cancer.

contact.silta: Who to contact in their region, a Finnish call script to read aloud, and their right to a free interpreter.
contact.src: IJERPH 2021;18(5):2229 (THL Maamu); Kuusio et al., BMC Health Serv Res 2022 (FinMonik).

fork.title: The public route is slower
fork.text: Patients who first went to a public health centre started treatment 84 days later than those who went to private or occupational care. The figure comes from one Finnish lymphoma study. Most people Silta serves start on the public route.
notes: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, 160 patients, 2014–2020. Grouped by first provider, not by language. Values read from the data labels of the study's slide.
fork.silta: Flash cards for showing symptoms, plus a Finnish summary the doctor can read at the first visit.
fork.src: Kuitunen et al., Cancer Medicine 2026;15:e71920 (Espoo talk, 13.11.2026).

visit.title: Understanding why a test was ordered
visit.text: Doctors sometimes order a test during a visit for something else, or at an occupational health check. No register shows how often this happens, or for whom.
visit.silta: It explains the test, the referral and the next steps in the person's language.
visit.src: Not reported in any source we found.

diag.title: Waiting for the diagnostic exam
diag.text: Waiting times are reported by county, not by language. They are longest in the capital region, where most other-language speakers live. All three routes meet here.
diag.silta: Silta cannot shorten the queue. It tells people what to expect and when to call if nothing arrives.
diag.src: Finnish Cancer Registry, “Delays in access to colonoscopy” and “Delays in access to diagnostic examinations”, 2024.

treat.title: Time to treatment
treat.text: None of the National Cancer Strategy's indicators split by native language, although Goal 3 sets target times for starting treatment.
treat.silta: What happens next, how long it usually takes, and when to call.

impact._about: The Impact view of /pathway: who is not reached and what it costs. Language is the main line; birth region, education and county sit beside it. Numbers from brain notes/2026-11-14-1630-silta-financial-lean-case.md, sources/2026-11-14-web-research-costs-and-funding.md, sources/2026-11-14-cancerregistry-screening-by-language.md and sources/data/2026-11-14-silta-cost-model.json.
impact.lede: One in four people invited to screening is not reached. The system pays for the invitation either way, and pays again at treatment when a cancer is found late.
impact.prompt: Select a step on the map to see what it costs.
impact.missing: We found no cost figure for this step.

letter.title: Every invitation is already paid for
letter.text: The three programmes sent 1,058,326 invitations in 2024, 78,914 of them to people whose native language is not Finnish, Swedish or Sámi. A breast screening invitation costs about €31 including the booked mammogram slot, paid whether or not the person comes. Unused breast slots are worth up to €1.95M a year, €0.30M of it for other-language invitees.
letter.src: Syöpäsäätiö / Nordic Healthcare Group cost statistics 2024 (breast screening €10.59M); Finnish Cancer Registry invitations 2024.

attend.title: 251,000 people not reached a year
attend.text: In 2024, 251,466 invited people did not attend screening: one in four. Reaching the national target of 80% in every programme takes about 45,000 more screenings a year (cervical and colorectal; breast is already at 81.6%), about €1.7M in screening costs. Language is the largest gap we can measure: if other-language invitees attended like Finnish and Swedish speakers, 16,561 more people would be screened.
attend.src: Finnish Cancer Registry 2024; programme costs from Syöpäsäätiö / NHG 2024, the STM screening decree memo and Virtanen et al. 2015.

follow.title: One in four skip the colonoscopy
follow.text: Nationally, 72.7% of people with a positive stool test had the colonoscopy in 2024. In the 2022 round, 87 colorectal cancers were found in people who tested positive but skipped it. Other-language invitees skip it more often: closing that gap means about 44 more colonoscopies a year, about €12,000. One cancer found at stage I instead of III avoids about €30,170 of treatment.
follow.src: THL Sotkanet indicator 6411; Finnish Cancer Registry 2022–24; THL unit cost 2024 (gastro outpatient visit, our proxy for a colonoscopy); Joranger et al., Eur J Health Econ 2020.

contact.title: About €460 to reach a specialist
contact.text: A nurse contact (€51), a doctor visit (€125) and a specialist outpatient visit (about €284) add up to about €460 of system cost before any imaging or tests. In Helsinki the person pays €71.30, for the specialist visit only.
contact.src: THL national unit costs 2024; City of Helsinki health service fees 2026.

fork.title: 84 more days for the cancer to grow
fork.text: The public route was 84 days slower to treatment in one lymphoma study. No study prices the delay itself. Its cost shows up at treatment, if the cancer has reached a later stage by then.

visit.title: The cheapest extra screening happens here
visit.text: Offering a self-sampling kit during a visit for something else costs about €45 per extra screening, close to a routine screening (€31). Reaching the same person by nurse phone calls costs about €360. In a London pilot, 56% took a kit offered at the visit and 65% returned it, against about 13% by post.
visit.src: Virtanen et al., BMC Women's Health 2015 (unit costs, 2012 prices); THL unit costs 2024; YouScreen pilot, London (133 practices).

diag.title: The wait has no price tag yet
diag.text: Waiting times are reported by county, not by language. Helsinki's median from a positive stool test to colonoscopy is 3.4 months, against 0.8 in the best counties. We found no cost for the wait itself.
diag.src: Finnish Cancer Registry, “Delays in access to colonoscopy”, 2024.

treat.title: Late diagnosis adds €15,000–30,000 per patient
treat.text: Breast cancer found after it has spread to the lymph nodes costs €15,100 more over 10 years than cancer found while local (€39,500 vs €24,400). Colorectal cancer found at stage III costs €30,170 more than at stage I (€56,800 vs €26,630). Kela and pension funds also paid €50M in sickness allowances and disability pensions for these two cancers in 2024.
treat.src: Lehtinen et al., Duodecim 2019 (specialist care, 2017 prices); Joranger et al., Eur J Health Econ 2020 (Norwegian model); Syöpäsäätiö / Nordic Healthcare Group 2024.

findings.label: people not reached a year
findings.text: One in four invited do not attend. Reaching 80% in every programme takes 45,000 more screenings a year.

findings.label: screenings missed a year
findings.text: 57 in 100 other-language invitees attend, against 78 in 100 Finnish and Swedish speakers.

findings.label: extra cost per patient found late
findings.text: Breast +€15,100 (spread to lymph nodes). Colorectal +€30,170 (stage III vs I).

findings.label: cost per extra screening
findings.text: Kit offered at a visit vs a nurse phoning. Only the €45 route pays for itself.

impact.summary: Reaching the 80% target in every programme means about 45,000 more screenings a year, about €1.7M in screening costs. Each cancer found before it spreads saves €15,000–30,000 of treatment. Language is the largest single gap we can measure, at 16,561 screenings a year. Helsinki already receives about €121M a year in state funding for its foreign-language residents, and none of it is earmarked.
